_about: The cross-reference index of the teachings. Read docs/cross-reference.md first. Concepts, page status and findings are kept by hand; fingerprints are stamped by scripts/check-content-index.py --record after the changed pages have been re-read against the index; mentions are worked out from the terms on every run.

Hinduism.note: "That thou art". Identity of self and ultimate reality is one school's reading of three.

Islam.note: The oneness of God, and God as the Light of the heavens and the earth.

Christianity.note: "You are the light of the world" and "God is light" are different sayings with different subjects.

Sikhism.note: One creator, and the Lord's Light within all.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: Only the perfect world God created truly exists.

Taoism.note: All things depend on the One. Zhuangzi's "all things and I are one" is at once undercut by its own author, so not a plain creed.

Judaism.note: The oneness of God, which is not the oneness of all existence.

Islam.note: Prayer, fasting and pilgrimage among the five.

Hinduism.note: Paths of action, knowledge and devotion for different temperaments. The fourfold scheme is Vivekananda's, from the winter of 1895 to 1896 (S190, read in snippets only; S58 is weaker).

Buddhism.note: The eightfold path; mindfulness of breathing as a path to liberation.

Christianity.note: Giving, prayer and fasting, done in secret.

Islam.note: Zakat, an obligation, and not only relief of the poor.

Christianity.note: The least of these; the merciful and the peacemakers.

Hinduism.note: Non-injury as a virtue. Not general pacifism.

Buddhism.note: Right speech and action; the five precepts.

Sikhism.note: Work for what you eat and give some of what you have.

Taoism.note: Gentleness, economy and not putting oneself first; contentment; against delighting in war, while allowing force under necessity. Not pacifism.

registers.label: How UPL speaks to its followers: belief, invitation, aspiration, commitment (five commitments)

Christianity.note: Classically marriage is between a man and a woman. Some churches now marry same-sex couples, with protection for those who dissent: the Episcopal Church and the Methodist Church in Britain. So "most churches, classically", not "Christianity".

Islam.note: Classical teaching: marriage between a man and a woman. 4:1 is the textual anchor; 30:21 alone does not establish it. A small number of progressive voices dissent.

Judaism.note: Classical law: a woman is betrothed to a man. The Reform movement affirms same-gender unions and leaves officiating to each rabbi; the Conservative movement approved rites in 2012 as distinct from classical betrothal. Orthodoxy does not permit them.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: Gratitude to parents and ancestors as a practice of the family.

Islam.note: The word and the teaching as the page uses it. Adam was forgiven, and no soul bears another's burden. Cite the verse; the hadith (S90) names other traditions.

Judaism.note: Made in the image of God; the soul placed within me is pure; no sin inherited from our ancestors. Judaism still teaches an inclination to evil.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: Already perfect, a child of God.

Buddhism.note: Buddha-nature is a Mahayana teaching of the potential for, or nature of, buddhahood in all beings. It is not a soul, it is not in early Buddhism in that form, and Mahayana schools disagree on what it is. Belief 4 names it in those terms.

Christianity.note: Original sin, stated three ways that must be kept apart. Catholic: a transmitted state, sin only by analogy and not a personal fault, nature wounded and not destroyed. Reformed: the guilt of the first sin imputed. Orthodox: mortality inherited, guilt not. Christianity also holds the image of God (S147).

Judaism.note: Love your neighbour, read with love the stranger; Hillel's rule, quoted whole.

Christianity.note: Jesus quotes Leviticus; the Samaritan widens the neighbour; love of enemies.

Islam.note: Against those who drive away the orphan; the merciful are shown mercy.

Buddhism.note: The Huayan school's net of Indra and Thich Nhat Hanh's interbeing. Early dependent origination (S74) explains the arising of suffering and only resembles this.

Hinduism.note: The whole world as a family: a late text about a detached sage.

Indigenous traditions.note: Māori kaitiakitanga; the Haudenosaunee Thanksgiving Address. Each is that people's own, not a general ethic.

Hawaiian tradition.note: Aloha ʻāina and mālama ʻāina, political as well as ecological.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: Grand Harmony of God, Nature, and Human Beings.

Bahá'í Faith.note: The oneness of humanity, one human family.

learning.label: Pursuit of knowledge and continuous learning

Islam.note: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge". The well-known hadith (S94) has a very weak chain.

Judaism.note: Study, and dispute for the sake of Heaven.

Buddhism.note: Test a teaching by its fruits and by what the wise praise. Not a licence to believe what one likes.

world-traditions.label: Respect for the wisdom of world traditions

Seicho-no-Ie.note: All religions emanate from one universal God. The nearest statement of UPL's own premise.

Islam.note: Honours earlier prophets and forbids compulsion in religion. Verses are read both inclusively (2:62) and exclusively (3:85); both are living positions and the page takes no side.

Hinduism.note: "To what is One, sages give many a title" names Vedic gods. Reading it as a statement about all religions is modern.

Buddhism.note: The teaching as a raft, a means and not an end. It is about the Buddha's own teaching, not about other religions.

Christianity.note: A range. Catholic teaching rejects nothing true and holy in other religions and holds that those who do not know Christ may be saved, always through Christ: inclusivist, not pluralist. The Reformed confession excludes. Universal restoration is a minority hope (S159). None of these says what UPL says.

Bahá'í Faith.note: The religions come from one source, as successive chapters of one religion. But Bahá'u'lláh is the latest Messenger with divine authority for this age, so it is not simple pluralism and must not be described as such.

Judaism.note: Chosenness is widely understood as responsibility and not superiority, though not by every Jewish thinker. Not a teaching about other religions.

Islam.note: Successors upon the earth, often understood as stewardship; do not be excessive.

Judaism.note: Do not destroy: a rabbinic extension of a verse on fruit trees. The environmental reading is modern.

Christianity.note: Francis of Assisi, patron of those who promote ecology, and his Canticle, which names Sir Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Wind, Sister Water, Brother Fire, Sister Mother Earth and Sister Bodily Death.

Indigenous traditions.note: Māori kaitiakitanga, a guardianship given by the local iwi to its own; the Mohawk Ohén:ton Karihwatéhkwen, "the words that come before all else". Each is that people's own and not a general ethic.

Buddhism.note: The Sangha: in the early texts the monastic order or the community of the awakened.

Christianity.note: Washing one another's feet; whoever would be great shall serve.

Sikhism.note: The shared meal open to all, and seva. Traditionally traced to Guru Nanak.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: The law of the mind: thought, word and deed shape the phenomenal world.

Islam.note: Gratitude; good character; ihsan; and taqwa, mindfulness of God, whose object is God and not the present moment. The author's claim that Islamic ethics encourage positive conduct and mindful awareness is sourced in this sense.

Buddhism.note: Mind or intention comes first, leading speech and action. It does not say thoughts create reality.

Christianity.note: Do not be anxious: trust, turning on "seek first God's Kingdom", not the power of thought.

Indigenous traditions.note: Thanks to each part of the natural world, said before anything important. Cite the Mohawk bodies (S188, S189) in place of the secondary S120.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: Reconciliation with all things; gratitude to ancestors. The English wording of the Grand Harmony message is not to be quoted yet.

Judaism.note: The waking prayer of thanks, and grace after meals.

Christianity.note: In everything give thanks; the psalms of thanksgiving.

Hinduism.note: A right to the work, not to its fruits.

Christianity.note: Done in secret, not for show.

Hinduism.note: From darkness lead me to light.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: The person as a child of God. UPL credits the phrase and keeps its own (decision D1).

Judaism.note: Humankind in the image of God. The verse does not say what the image is; the mystical teaching of divine sparks is not recorded here and is to be described, not absorbed.

Buddhism.note: Early Buddhism denies a creator, not the gods, and rejects the view that a creator causes all we experience because it removes responsibility. The poisoned arrow (S128) is about speculation in general and does not mention a creator.

Taoism.note: The Tao of the Tao Te Ching is a source before Heaven and Earth, "the Mother of all things", and not a personal creator. Near to UPL's impersonal source. Later religious Daoism has gods.

Judaism.note: The Shema. "The Eternal alone" in the current JPS, exclusive loyalty; "the Lord is one" is the liturgical reading. A personal God, which UPL's is not.

Islam.note: The oneness of God, and God as light. A personal God, which UPL's is not.

Taoism.note: Legge's wording for the three things to hold dear is gentleness, economy and not taking precedence. Laozi may be legendary.

Sikhism.note: The three teachings and the langar are traditionally attributed to him. Cite years only for his dates.

soul.label: The immortal soul (also spirit, consciousness of the person, true self)

Seicho-no-Ie.note: Man is not matter but spiritual existence.

Buddhism.note: Nothing in body or mind is a permanent, unchanging self, and Buddha-nature is explicitly not a soul. UPL parts from Buddhism here and says so (decision D3).

Christianity.note: The soul is immortal, but the hope is the resurrection of the body, with which the soul is reunited. UPL's cocoon image, a body left behind, differs.

Islam.note: The spirit is breathed into the human being; the classical teaching is bodily resurrection and judgement. 17:85 may not be about the human soul at all.

Judaism.note: The soul placed within me is pure.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: The silkworm and the cocoon, from the Nectarean Shower of Holy Doctrines.

Judaism.note: Teshuvah, return: a wrong done to a person is mended by making it good and seeking forgiveness. It is about repair, not about cause and effect.

Hawaiian tradition.note: Hoʻoponopono sets right what has gone wrong within a family. Repair, not cause and effect.

Hinduism.note: One's own dharma is bound to the four classes in the text. UPL takes the path of right action and not the assignment by birth.

Buddhism.note: In Buddhism the dharma is the teaching and the truth it points to. The same word, a different sense.

Christianity.note: Eternal punishment is classical teaching, Catholic and Protestant. Orthodoxy speaks of hell as the experience of God's love by those who reject it. Universal restoration, held by Gregory of Nyssa, is a minority hope the confessions condemn. UPL does not teach eternal punishment.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: The author's source for these pages: a person leaves the body-cocoon and rises to the world of spirit, and the essence of a person is life. The sutra's "death is not real" means, on the author's reading, that death is not the end: it seems final, and it is not. No difference from UPL on death; the difference is on illness (see Science and modern medicine).

Hinduism.note: The soul lays aside a worn-out body as worn-out clothes, and takes another. The verse teaches rebirth, which UPL has not yet defined.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: A person is not matter, not the body, not the cells of the brain or the nerves.

Hinduism.note: The soul is not destroyed when the body is destroyed.

Hawaiian tradition.note: Hoʻoponopono is a way of setting relationships right more than a meditation.

Christianity.note: Lectio Divina, four steps and then action; the Jesus Prayer, which asks for a spiritual guide; centering prayer, a method of the 1970s that some Catholics criticise. Not on any page yet.
The Lord's Prayer, without the later doxology.
Allegorical reading: one major strand, and Augustine warns against it as well as for it.

Hinduism.note: The Upanishads teach by dialogue, a teacher answering a student.

Sikhism.note: No intoxicant, in the Sikh code of conduct.

Judaism.note: Saving a life comes before almost every other duty.

Christianity.note: Healing with a word, read as teaching about faith and not as a technique.

Seicho-no-Ie.note: In the True Image there is no disease. UPL holds that illness is real and is treated (decisions D1 and D2).

Bahá'í Faith.note: Religion and science as the two wings on which human intelligence soars.

Hawaiian tradition.note: To set right: a family process led by a respected mediator. The four-phrase form is a modern adaptation.

findings.note: Resolved 21 September 2026 by decision D2 and proposals P1 and P2: the introduction now says "trust in science and modern medicine", and the page states that UPL heals the spirit, medicine treats the body, and a follower never relies on spiritual or alternative remedies alone.

Resolved 21 September 2026 by decision D1 and proposals P4 to P9: God is not a person but the source of light. Comparative Analysis and the God page now say so, "God's love" is explained as the nature of the light, "divine will" became "divine order", and prayer is attunement. Unity still describes Tawhid in Islam's own terms, which is a description of Islam and not of UPL's God.

Resolved 21 September 2026 by decision D3 and proposal P3: Comparative Analysis now honours the Buddha's teaching that suffering can be understood and ended, and states openly that UPL parts from Buddhism on the self.
Resolved 21 September 2026 by proposal P64: Purpose now says "UPL's purpose pivots around", so the mission is stated once, on Name, Mission, and Vision.
Resolved 21 September 2026: the practice section links to the core belief, and by proposal P65 the core belief links to the section, so a reader can tell the statement from its elaboration.
Resolved 21 September 2026: the way-of-life section links to the core belief, and by proposal P66 the core belief links to the section.

Resolved 21 September 2026 by proposal P24. The core belief now states the concept in general, "nothing in existence stands alone, and… to learn is to discover how things are joined", and credits the Huayan school and Thich Nhat Hanh for it. The environmental page remains its application to nature.

Resolved 21 September 2026 by proposal P67: the page is retitled An Open Practice, which is what its paragraph describes. The file name and address are unchanged. If the author later names the practices a list would hold, the page can take its old title back.

The silkworm and cocoon image is given in full on both pages, a result of splitting the paper. The image is now credited on The Immortal Soul to Taniguchi's Nectarean Shower of Holy Doctrines (source S07).
findings.reason: Accepted by the author on 21 September 2026. The three sentences do different jobs: the section introduction keeps the author's original sentence, The Immortal Soul gives the image in full with its credit and owns it, and the Death page reports what the sutra says.

findings.note: Resolved 21 September 2026: each subsection now points to the other. A page listing the observances waits for the author to name them (parked in the tradition balance plan).
Resolved 21 September 2026: the Gratitude section owns the definition, and Positive Thinking and the Power of Gratefulness now links to it. No existing wording changed.
Ho'oponopono is glossed as reconciliation and forgiveness on both pages.
findings.reason: Accepted by the author on 21 September 2026. The section introduction glosses the practice in a few words and the dedicated page owns it. The introduction's spelling now takes the ʻokina, as the page title does.

The section introduction lists the four sources of ethics that the page under it then treats one by one.
findings.reason: An introduction that previews its section. Keep the two lists in step.

findings.note: The home page, the Abstract and the Conclusion each summarise the whole. The home page's first sentence repeats the Abstract's.
findings.reason: These are the summary pages of the founding paper. A change of doctrine must be carried into all three.

findings.note: The site configuration holds its own one-paragraph summary of the religion, used in llms.txt and structured data. It is a description, not a teaching, but it is doctrine-shaped text outside content/ and can drift from it.
findings.reason: Machine-facing metadata, allowed by locked decision 3. Re-read it whenever the home page or the Abstract changes.

findings.note: Resolved 21 September 2026 by proposal P21. Both pages gave Seicho-No-Ie's teaching on the child of God in nearly the same words. The God page now says "a being of spirit and not of matter", and "already perfect" stays with belief 4, where it is about innate goodness.
